content: Travelers to areas where wild polioviruses and diphtheria are present should ensure immunity to poliomyelitis and diphtheria. Unvaccinated adults traveling to developing countries or regions with endemic polio should receive at least two doses of enhanced inactivated poliovirus vaccine (eIPV) spaced one month apart, ideally completing a full primary vaccination series before travel. eIPV is preferred for adults due to a slightly higher risk of vaccine-associated paralysis compared to children. If time does not allow for the full interval, a single dose of either oral poliovirus vaccine (OPV) or eIPV is recommended. Adults who have been partially vaccinated with OPV or inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV) should complete the remaining doses of their primary series, regardless of the time elapsed since the last dose or the type of vaccine previously received. Travelers who have completed a primary OPV series should receive a single supplementary dose of OPV, while those who completed a primary IPV series should receive a single supplementary dose of either OPV or eIPV. The necessity for additional doses of either vaccine has not been established. Individuals at increased risk of complications from influenza, such as those traveling to the tropics at any time of year or to the Southern Hemisphere between April and September, should review their influenza vaccination history. If they were not vaccinated during the previous fall or winter, they should consider receiving the influenza vaccine before travel. High-risk individuals should be strongly encouraged to receive the most current vaccine available. Those who received the previous season’s vaccine in preparation for travel should be revaccinated in the fall or winter with the current vaccine, potentially receiving two doses of influenza vaccine within one year. Selective vaccination of travelers with vaccines against yellow fever, cholera, typhoid, plague, meningococcal disease, rabies, or hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, or the administration of immune globulin (IG) to prevent hepatitis A, is recommended based on the specific disease risks in the destination country and the type and duration of travel. For cholera and yellow fever, vaccination requirements may be mandated by the destination country. Information on known or potentially infected areas is published annually in Health Information for International Travel, which also lists specific vaccination requirements for cholera and yellow fever for each country. These publications are available through state and local health departments or by contacting the CDC Information Services. For entry into countries requiring yellow fever or cholera vaccination, travelers must possess a validated International Certificate of Vaccination. State or local health departments can provide information on authorized centers for certificate validation. Additional details on vaccine-preventable illnesses that travelers may encounter are available in sections describing specific vaccines. Foreign students, immigrants, and refugees entering the United States may be susceptible to diseases such as diphtheria, tetanus, measles, mumps, rubella, and poliomyelitis, as routine vaccination against these diseases is not universal in many countries. Those from regions with high HBV prevalence, such as Southeast Asia, should be screened for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and antibodies (anti-HBs). Susceptible household and sexual contacts of HBsAg carriers should receive the HBV vaccine. Unless vaccination records or laboratory evidence of immunity are provided, foreign students, immigrants, and refugees should receive age-appropriate vaccines as outlined in the Age Groups section. Certain vaccines may be contraindicated for individuals with specific health conditions, while others may be indicated due to underlying health issues. A summary of immunobiologics recommended or contraindicated for individuals with selected health problems is provided in the relevant sections. For pregnant women, vaccination or toxoid administration should ideally be delayed until the second or third trimester to minimize concerns about potential teratogenicity. Pregnant women not previously vaccinated against tetanus and diphtheria should receive two properly spaced doses of tetanus-diphtheria (Td) vaccine. Those who have received one or two doses of tetanus or diphtheria toxoid should complete their primary series during pregnancy. A primary series consists of three doses of diphtheria and tetanus toxoids, with the first two doses given at least four weeks apart and the third dose administered 6–12 months after the second. Pregnant women who have completed a primary series should receive a Td booster if more than 10 years have elapsed since their last dose. Live-virus vaccines are generally contraindicated during pregnancy due to theoretical risks to the developing fetus. However, if immediate protection against poliomyelitis or yellow fever is required due to imminent exposure, OPV or yellow fever vaccine may be administered. If vaccination with the yellow fever vaccine is solely for international travel requirements, efforts should be made to obtain a waiver letter. The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) strongly recommends administering the rubella vaccine postpartum to women not known to be immune, preferably before hospital discharge. Data on the safety of HBV vaccines for the developing fetus are not available.
